newsitem.title: POLAND: INTERNAL ROW ROCKS MAIN POLISH OPPOSITION GROUP.
newsitem.headline: INTERNAL ROW ROCKS MAIN POLISH OPPOSITION GROUP.

text.p: A struggle among the 45 groupings in Poland's largest opposition bloc neared a climax on Wednesday as chiefs of Solidarity Election Action (AWS) drafted lists of candidates for this year's polls.
The Solidarity trade union has forged the squabbling small parties of the right into a bloc with a real chance of beating the ruling ex-communists in elections due in September.

But as final decisions approached on which politicians from member parties would get the coveted top places on ballot papers around the country, some parties said they might quit AWS if they and their policies were not adequately represented.
Solidarity union spokesman Piotr Zak said he did not expect any major defections that might weaken the AWS, saying most such politicians would face oblivion outside the AWS umbrella.

"There is no danger, in my view, that AWS will fall apart," Zak told Reuters as a six-member committee of the alliance, including four trade union representatives, met at a secret location near Warsaw putting final touches to the lists.
"Some party political leaders are just fighting for their personal and party interests," he said, adding that no statement on the outcome was expected until Thursday.
Lech Walesa, who founded Solidarity amid the struggle against communist rule in 1980 and was Poland's president from 1990 to 1995, condemned any actions that could split AWS.
"Everyone who steps out against unity can expect to be hit strongly by me," Walesa, who is keeping a back seat in politics but retains influence in parts of the right, told Reuters.

The row over party lists stems largely from concerns that the trade union is reserving too many of the plum high positions on ballot papers for its own members or its closest allies on the Christian, nationalist right of AWS.
Solidarity denies it is taking a disproportionate share.

Although AWS last month agreed on its election programme outlines, the rows also involve policy issues, pitting often populist radical right-wingers against more liberal pro-market groups in the AWS whose presence might lure in centrist voters.
Several AWS members are strongly resisting union efforts to transform the alliance of 37 parties and some other groups into a single political party.

In a newspaper interview on Wednesday Czeslaw Bielecki, head of the centre-right Ruch Stu (100 Movement) in the AWS, said his party was not willing to pay any cost to remain in the alliance, but refused to lay out his terms for remaining.

The personal and policy rivalries fracturing Poland's right, descended from parts of the pre-1989 opposition to communist rule, contributed to their rout in 1993 elections at the hands of their old foes the former communists.
Opinion polls suggest that grouped in AWS they now provide the best hope for voters wanting to unseat the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).
A survey by the private Demoskop institute published on Tuesday showed AWS and SLD running level with 21 percent support each.
The centrist opposition Union for Freedom (UW) and the Peasant party which now shares power with the ex-communists, tied with 13 percent each.
